https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Pete Hegseth has presided over unprecedented upheaval at the Pentagon that does not appear to have enhanced national defense capabilities. Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AP View image in fullscreen Pete Hegseth has presided over unprecedented upheaval at the Pentagon that does not appear to have enhanced national defense capabilities. Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Pete Hegseth Captain calamity: Pete Hegseth under fire for ‘inept’ leadership of US military The US defense secretary faces internal dissent and discord at the Pentagon, accused of focusing on culture war issues and his own political ambitions as the Iran war drags on Robert Tait in Washington Sat 5 Sep 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 06.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I n a different Washington, under a different president, a return to the well-worn playbook of all-out sanctions to counter Iran might have been the signal for a publicity-hungry US secretary of defense to adopt a lower profile. But these are no ordinary times. And Pete Hegseth is no ordinary defense secretary. Barely a week after the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, unleashed a supposed “economic D-day” aimed at crushing the regime in Tehran under the weight of commercial pressures, Hegseth once again returned to the limelight – and the center of controversy. The former Fox News host usurped Bessent from center stage as the conflict with Iran reverted to open warfare and discontent at the Pentagon was laid bare once more. Democrats warn of ‘hollowed out’ leadership after army chief resigns amid clashes with Hegseth Read more Turf wars within Hegseth’s own fiefdom resurfaced with the resignation of the army secretary, fresh revelations of blocked promotions and leaked disclosures of resistance from military top brass of extended deployments to the Middle East. While the Pentagon insists that any suggestion the defense department is in disarray under Hegseth is “completely baseless”, alarm over his conduct in the role – and the implications – has not merely been expressed by Hegseth’s political opponents. “The secretary of defense is a clear and present danger to the national security of the United States and the world,” said Randy Manner, a retired major general in the US national guard – in which Hegseth also served – and member of National Security Leaders for America (NSL4A), a group of former military leaders. “He has done more harm to the national security of the United States than any secretary of defense since the country was created.” Thom Tillis, the Republican senator from North Carolina, who is stepping down from the US Senate after clashes with Donald Trump, bluntly urged the US president this week to fire his defense secretary. “I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis wrote on social media. “He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and wellbeing of our fighting force.” After a month-long lull, the resumption of strikes on Iranian targets near the strait of Hormuz meanwhile renewed questions over just what the US wants to achieve in its war with the Islamic regime, which Trump and his defense secretary once loudly vowed to topple. The strikes, on mainland Iran as well as Iranian islands in the Gulf, caused multiple casualties. In one incident, Iranian media reported that five people, including a six-year-old child, were killed in the southern city of Kuhestak when a missile struck a wedding party. Iranian authorities labelled the deaths a war crime. The episode had echoes of strikes in the city of Minab on the first day of the war on 28 February, when more than 150 people, including 120 children, were killed when missiles hit an elementary school. The US has not formally admitted responsibility, although officials have said the incident is under military investigation. The latest strikes were quickly followed by disclosures that Hegseth had extended military deployments in the Middle East , where the US currently maintains 50,000 troops and 19 warships – partly to enforce a naval blockade on Iran – into the middle of next year The extensions were ordered even after several commanders in other sectors voiced objections, formally known as “non-concurs”, to the deployments, arguing that they could leave the US at risk of being unable to meet its commitments in other areas, while subjecting forces to the additional strain of being at sea for too long. The non-concurs were recorded in the Secretary of Defense Orders Book of 14 August, a classified document whose contents were leaked and reported by the Washington Post . ‘The past six months has failed’ “I’m not sure what the strategy is here,” Kevin Carroll, a former army colonel and military intelligence officer who served in the offices of the defense secretary and joint chiefs of staff, said of the war on Iran. “What’s the enemy’s center of gravity that we’re going after? “We tried decapitating their leadership. That didn’t work. We tried going after their missile program. We were not able to destroy it. Tried sinking the navy, but they still maintain a mining capability. “We could easily take out their energy infrastructure. But that would drive the price of oil much, much higher, and lead to retaliatory attacks on the energy infrastructure of our Gulf allies. It’s not clear what this target set is intended to do.” Nate Swanson, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a former White House and state department adviser on Iran, said Hegseth’s long-term deployment orders reflected the administration’s decision to embrace a policy of long-term economic blockade. “It’s a recognition of the fact that the past six months has failed, but they don’t know what to do,” argued Swanson, who suggested that Trump was attracted by the idea of abandoning the conflict, but wanted to do so in way that enabled him to project strength. As the war drags on, Hegseth stands accused of being insufficiently engaged with such grave policy matters, preferring instead to focus on “cultural” issues – sacrificing the careers of talented career officers in the process – and his future political ambitions. The defense secretary, who has evaded awkward questions or scrutiny by not holding a formal Pentagon briefing since 5 May, has reportedly told associates that he is considering a bid for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination. In the midst of a burgeoning trade war between the US and Canada, Hegseth – who has previously railed against “fat” generals and instituted testosterone tests for service personnel – found time to wade in by apparently “body shaming” two Canadian female teenage cadets . The social media post attracted a storm of criticism. In a podcast , Joe Walsh, a former Republican congressman who is now a Democrat, accused Hegseth of “fucking online harassment” and denounced the defense secretary as a “punk”. Tensions over Hegseth’s priorities reached a head this week when the army secretary, Dan Driscoll – a friend and ally of Vice-President JD Vance – resigned after repeatedly clashing with Hegseth over blocked promotions and purges of senior commanders on flimsy pretexts. The rest of the military is significantly degraded. A large proportion of those blocked or fired have been black or female, in line with Hegseth’s vocal crusade against “woke” DEI (diversity, equity and inclusiveness) initiatives. In the latest of a series of purges, the New York Times reported that Hegseth had blocked the promotions of seven officers to the two-star general rank. In submitting his resignation, Driscoll – who has spearheaded efforts to modernize the army, including through embracing drone warfare – voiced concerns “surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the generals who were responsible”, a source told CNN . Driscoll’s departure – and the reasons for it – aroused anger even among Republicans, most notably Tillis, the outgoing GOP senator. “Dan was the right man at the right moment to lead our Soldiers and Army civilians,” wrote Tillis. The withering verdict is seconded by some retired generals, who say misgivings over Hegseth’s leadership are quietly shared by many serving officers who remain. Manner said Hegseth was depriving other parts of the armed forces to fund the Iran war out of “readiness accounts”. “These are for training the rest of the force,” he said. “So the rest of the force is losing training hours, equipment and money for maintenance and operations. The rest of the military is significantly degraded.” Manner also said his conversations with serving officers bore out the leaked concerns voiced in the Secretary of Defence’s Orders Book. “I have firsthand knowledge of people who are serving on active duty who echo the exact same concerns that we are headed to a situation where we can no longer defend Taiwan, that we are very unlikely to be able to defend even, quite frankly, South Korea,” he said. ‘Infinitely worse’ than Rumsfeld Hegseth, who has drawn accusations of war crimes for ordering a succession of strikes on alleged drug-ferrying boats off the coasts of South America, is not the first US defense secretary to come under a harsh spotlight over the conduct of a far-off American war. Robert McNamara, defense secretary under Lyndon Johnson, became a lightning rod for criticism during the Vietnam war before eventually undergoing a crisis of conscience and being moved to a new role as head of the International Monetary Fund. During George W Bush’s administration, Donald Rumsfeld became the target of fierce criticism after failing as defense secretary to plan adequately for the occupation of Iraq after the initial invasion to topple Saddam Hussein. But Paul Eaton, a retired major general who trained Iraqi troops after the invasion and is now an adviser to VoteVets – an advocacy group for progressive military veterans – said Rumsfeld’s failings paled in comparison with Hegseth. If you fail to plan, plan to fail, and what we’re seeing in the Iran war is is just evidence “Rumsfeld had ‘next war-itis’, which was a contributing factor to Bush firing him after the shellacking that the Republican party had in the [2006] midterms,” Eaton said. “All this sounds faintly familiar with what we’re going through right now. “But this is infinitely worse because we had a lot of other very smart people to corral the bad ideas coming out of Rumsfeld. [This time] we’ve had the whole removal of seasoned men and women who have learned things the hard way most of the time in combat. “If you fail to plan, plan to fail, and what we’re seeing in the Iran war is just evidence. The frustration is, we’re better than this in the uniformed military but we got handed a terrible set of guidance from our civilian leadership.” Michael O’Hanlon, a defense and strategy expert at the Brookings Institution, argued that the armed forces had enough “bench strength” to survive Hegseth’s purges without imminent collapse, but lamented the loss of certain key individuals who could not be easily replaced. He singled out Gen Chris Donahue, who recently stepped down from his post as head of the US land command in Europe and Africa. “We haven’t had a TV talkshow star with a strong partisan and cultural agenda wind up as secretary of defense,” said O’Hanlon. “There may be some echoes of previous secretaries, but the political and culture stuff is Pete Hegseth through and through.” Hegseth was “not going to wind up leaving a major mark”, O’Hanlon predicted. “He’s going to wind up being known as the guy who fought Trump’s culture wars for him – and maybe failed to help Trump stay out of trouble in the Iran war, depending on how bad that gets.” Explore more on these topics Pete Hegseth US politics US-Israel war on Iran US military Trump administration features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://reason.com/2026/08/29/9-11-turbo.text: Like many others in the Washington, D.C., or New York metro areas, my experience of 9/11 was horrifying and yet unremarkable at the same time. I was a 16-year-old British student spending a year in an American high school in Arlington, Virginia, just a few miles from the Pentagon. That Tuesday morning dawned like any other. It was sunny and warm; D.C. was experiencing its traditional third or fourth blast of summer heat well into September. In second period, someone flipped on the TV, which was showing images of a plane disaster in New York. Tragic, but hardly cause to break routine. The band teacher flipped it back off and returned to teaching. It wasn't long, though, before things went off the rails. While walking to my next class, there was a commotion down the hall: someone screaming, the hysterical sound bouncing off the tiled corridor. I would later learn that a girl was trying to reach her parents at work in the Pentagon—and failing. By the time the principal made the announcement that school was closed, rumors and panic had begun to spread throughout the student body. Things after that are a disconnected blur. Waiting in classrooms for parents to come and collect students without transportation; some arrived crying. My mother managed to get a phone line and briefly call me. She was trapped on a Metro platform, the trains disgorging all their passengers and going out of service. Even the television news was frenetic and unclear: Another plane was headed for the White House. No, it was headed for CIA headquarters in McLean. There are car bombs downtown. The president has been taken to a secret location. One classmate's father, who worked at the Pentagon, saw the crash in his rearview mirror as he drove to a dentist's appointment. My mother finally made it to school and took me home. It would take several more hours for my father, who worked mere blocks from the White House, to arrive: Like many others, he had been forced to walk out of Washington, across the bridges, and through miles of suburbs to get home. These experiences remain etched in my mind, horrible enough to be fresh even all these years later, and yet they were in no way unique. In the days, months, and years to follow, I would hear so many distinct variants of the same story: a group of students on a trip who'd seen the plane as it descended toward the building; a classmate whose father was whisked away by government helicopter to some unknown location, leaving them to wonder where he was; a think-tanker whose child attended an on-site daycare at the Pentagon. I kept thinking back to that last story after I became a mother myself. Could I even imagine the panic and terror of a parent in that situation? It's tempting to look back at the shock and horror of 9/11, a trauma shared by much of Washington's foreign policy class, as the genesis of many foreign policy mistakes that would follow. Hurt people, as the saying goes, hurt people. And as the events of the following years unfurled—the toppling of the Taliban, the invasion of Iraq, the internments at Guantánamo Bay, the passage of the USA PATRIOT Act, and so on—it became tempting to blame it all on that singular day of pain and horror. But as we approach the 25th anniversary of the attacks, it's important to understand the limits of that story. The events of 9/11 undoubtedly had a major impact on foreign policy. Yet this impact was less a change of direction and more an intensification of already existing trends. The 9/11 attacks would create a permissive political and psychological environment for a particular foreign policy vision, but it did not set America on the path to liberal interventionism and forever war all by itself. For that, we must look back into the 1990s. The Unipolar Moment The collapse of the Soviet Union unchained America. Economic and social malaise had been undermining the USSR for decades, as an aging parade of apparatchiks presided over stagnation and discontent. The rise of Mikhail Gorbachev and a sudden, unexpected series of arms-control agreements brought an era of détente, while a series of popular revolutions in Eastern Europe severed the USSR from its Eastern bloc dependencies. By the time the Soviet flag was lowered on the Kremlin walls on Christmas Day 1991, it was clear to all involved that America had won the Cold War. This outcome raised hopes in Washington of a better world. As President George H.W. Bush told Congress, the dawning of something better might be visible: "Out of these troubled times, our fifth objective—a new world order—can emerge….An era in which the nations of the world, East and West, North and South, can prosper and live in harmony." The Soviet collapse, leaving America as the only superpower, offered policymakers a chance to use America's overwhelming power to build that better world. The end of the Cold War was thus marked not only with a sense of righteous victory, but also with a feeling in Washington that a new foreign policy consensus needed to be forged. The early 1990s was nicknamed the " Kennan Sweepstakes ." Thinkers vied to become the next George Kennan, whose 1946 telegram created a doctrine for the Cold War, with new missions and new rationales for U.S. foreign policy. The bipartisan consensus that emerged married Republican primacists and neoconservatives to Democratic liberal internationalists around a form of " liberal hegemony ." What united these groups was a conviction that America—the "indispensable nation"—could transform the world into something better, whether that was by toppling prospective enemies of the United States or engaging in humanitarian intervention. Each administration from Bill Clinton to at least Barack Obama held it as an article of faith that if America could make the world more interconnected and more liberal , it could also make the world more peaceful. U.S. foreign policy thus became increasingly assertive. It is an oft-forgotten irony that George W. Bush was elected in 2000 promising to reject excessive humanitarian intervention and nation building, sentiments that helped him to win the Republican nomination over noted hawk John McCain. The nation building in question was President Clinton's repeated interventions in the Balkans, designed to prevent atrocities in the former Yugoslavia. Crimes like the mass killing at Srebrenica in the 1990s led U.S. officials to embrace the "responsibility to protect"—the notion that if a state did not or could not protect its own citizens, the international community was obliged to intervene to protect civilians. In practice, "the international community" meant the United States. Indeed, when conflict broke out between Serbian forces and Kosovar separatists, the Clinton administration ran an air campaign not with the approval of the U.N. Security Council, where Russian and Chinese vetoes prevented action, but under the auspices of NATO. The campaign forced Serbia to accept a peace deal and in effect created a new country in Kosovo. Other elements of U.S. foreign policy under Clinton were similarly ambitious and transformative. His administration engaged in strenuous negotiations with Congress over the admission of China to the World Trade Organization. Concerns about China's growing economy and undemocratic government were smoothed over by the notion that greater trade and interdependence could bring greater global stability in the long run. By bringing China into the community of nations in this way, it was believed, China's rise could be managed, turning it into a "responsible stakeholder" in the existing American-led order. Then there was NATO expansion. With the collapse of the USSR, NATO no longer had an enemy to protect against, raising the possibility that the alliance was obsolete. But as early as George H.W. Bush's administration, U.S. policymakers demanded that a unified Germany stay in NATO, inherently implying that the pact still had a role to play in European security. It was the Clinton administration that suggested that NATO might also have a place for the countries of the former Warsaw Pact. By the end of his term, Clinton had authorized the first round of NATO expansion and set the stage for more. NATO expansion was increasingly seen as a way to lock in stability, democracy, and economic reform in Eastern Europe. NATO's expansion was coupled with an American push to expand its scope, transforming it from a deterrence force inside Europe to a global peacekeeping army that could act when the United Nations could not. More than 60,000 NATO-associated troops participated in the Bosnian implementation and stabilization efforts that followed the Dayton Peace Accords of 1995. What tied many of these Clinton-era policies together was the aim of prolonging the post–Cold War period of American predominance over both allies and adversaries. One way this manifested itself was the idea that the United States should not withdraw from European security, keeping European allies purposefully weak. Another way was a policy of "dual containment" against both Iraq and Iran. Across the 1990s, the U.S. would sustain a no-fly zone over Iraq, enforce U.N. sanctions on Iraqi oil, and engage in several bombing campaigns against Iraqi military targets and to protect civilians in Kurdish areas. As we exited the 1990s, American policymakers were riding high. No challengers were on the horizon, proto–rogue states like Iraq were contained, and globalization and liberalization were flourishing around the world. Perhaps nothing exemplified the mood surrounding U.S. foreign policy better than a declaration by Madeleine Albright, Clinton's secretary of state: "If we have to use force, it is because we are America; we are the indispensable nation. We stand tall and we see further than other countries into the future." At home, the president might have been embroiled in a sex scandal, but abroad, America's destiny as leader and prophet of the post–Cold War world seemed assured. Turbocharged It was in this messianic ground that the seeds of 9/11 were sown. An introspective observer might have wondered how the nation who "saw further into the future" had so disastrously missed the threat from Al Qaeda. Future inquiries would conclude that the attacks would not have been possible without serious lapses in both Clinton and Bush's counterterrorism policies, as well as institutional and intelligence failures. The 9/11 attacks were clearly terror and barbarism; thousands of grieving American families at funerals proved that beyond any doubt. But they were also a challenge to America's post–Cold War image. A terrorist group had been able to hatch a plan in caves in one of the world's poorest and most isolated countries (never mind that most of the actual plotting and preparation had taken place in Germany!), turning the very tools of global connectivity against America. The attacks came to be seen as an affront to America's new world—a challenge to the forces of civilized, liberal order. Photo: U.S. Army soldiers search travelers in Afghanistan on March 9, 2012; Sgt. Ken Scar/7th Mobile Public Affairs Detachment The invasion of Afghanistan was a logical and justified response to the attacks. The Taliban had sheltered Al Qaeda and its leader, Osama bin Laden; they had, in a very real sense, declared war on the United States. The toppling of the Taliban was swift and merciless. Less than three months after the attacks, Kabul was conquered and an interim Afghan government was in place. But in the atmosphere of the time, mere military victory was not enough. Bin Laden and many of his top lieutenants were still at large. "Rogue states" such as Iran, Iraq, Syria, and North Korea might need to be deterred. Other "ungoverned spaces" might pose a similar threat in future. In response, the Bush administration formulated the "freedom agenda," a hugely ambitious strategy that sought to address all of these problems at their root. This freedom agenda turned the war in Afghanistan into an exercise in modernization and nation building, which was used to sell a separate war of regime change in Iraq. In each case, U.S. military power was to transform whole societies. Iraq and Afghanistan were prototypes, proving grounds for the idea that a democratization campaign could act as a catalyst for change across the whole of the Middle East. "The great strength of this nation," the 2002 U.S. National Security Strategy document put it, "must be used to promote a balance of power that favors freedom." Though U.S. public opinion began to turn decisively against the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan as Bush's presidency ended, his successors continued to pursue similarly transformative goals on the world stage. President Barack Obama, for example, had come into office promising to pull back from the global war on terror, but he ended up surging troops into both Afghanistan and Iraq. His administration also engaged in regime change in Libya and covert intervention in Syria. Obama was building not just on Bush's freedom agenda but on the Clinton administration's invocation of the responsibility to protect. Several of Obama's foreign policy advisers—Hillary Clinton, Samantha Power, Susan Rice—were true believers in using U.S. power to protect human rights and spread democracy. As the Arab Spring crashed across the Middle East in 2011 and mass protests in Libya spilled into open civil war, the administration authorized a NATO-led campaign that quickly advanced from a no-fly zone designed to protect civilians to an open campaign of regime change. Photo: A car bombing in Iraq in 2005; U.S. Army SPC Ronald Shaw Jr./DOD Defense Visual Information Center America's Middle East interventions after 9/11 even bolstered its other ambitious post–Cold War policies. For example, NATO now had more impetus to focus on expeditionary and "out of area" capabilities. The alliance played an active role in the International Security Assistance Force process in Afghanistan and then in the Libya campaign. NATO expansion and the war on terror would become practically symbiotic: For newer members, providing political support and token military forces in Iraq and Afghanistan was viewed as a quid pro quo for membership, while the sacrifices made by their soldiers became a justification for that membership. The Hangover Public disillusionment with all of these policies grew throughout the 2000s and 2010s. By 2016, Donald Trump was reaching swing voters by declaring the Iraq War a mistake; by 2020, Democratic primary candidates would be pledging en masse to extricate the U.S. from the Middle East. Twenty-five years after 9/11, elements of the war on terror still linger across the Middle East and, increasingly, Africa—and the war is generally viewed as a failure. The Middle East became less a proving ground for democracy and human rights promotion, and more a graveyard for the notion that freedom can be built at the point of a gun. Yet with 25 years of space, it also becomes easier to see how the war on terror fits into the broader trajectory of post–Cold War U.S. foreign policy. America's response to 9/11 turbocharged many of its worst impulses but did not fundamentally change its direction. The zeal of the indispensable nation mixed with the shock of a large-scale terrorist attack—one experienced firsthand by many of Washington's foreign policy elites—created a permissive environment in which ambitious theories of global peace and change could flourish. The war on terror is simply the best-known and most visible of the transformative impulses that characterized the post–Cold War pursuit of liberal hegemony. Would regime-change wars in Iraq or Libya have happened without 9/11? Would America have spent two decades bogged down in the Middle East, wasting blood and treasure while China rose quietly? Perhaps not. But a quarter-century later, we should ask ourselves how much of what followed the 9/11 attacks stemmed from shared trauma and

Photograph: Andrew O’Connor/Australian Broadcasting Corp/AP Western Australia Shark catch-and-kill order issued after swimmer dies off popular Perth beach Man, 63, fatally bitten by shark at Sorrento beach on Friday morning Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Achol Arok and Kat Wong Sat 19 Sep 2026 02.43 EDT First published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 03.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A shark that fatally attacked a man on a beach in Perth’s north will be “destroyed” if it is captured, after an order was issued by the Western Australian government. As the hunt for the animal remained under way on Saturday, the WA fisheries minister, Jackie Jarvis, revealed she had greenlit the order. “Given the shark had been positively identified, remained in the vicinity following a fatal attack and was considered to pose an ongoing threat, I authorised fisheries officers to destroy the shark if captured,” she said in a social media post. Rabbits are the biggest threat to Australia’s native species. Why are their numbers booming again? Read more Emergency services were called to the popular Sorrento beach at about 10.30am on Friday after reports of a shark-related incident. Western Australia police said a 63-year-old man had been bitten by a shark while swimming along the coast. He died as a result of his injuries, police said. Emergency services, including water and air personnel, conducted an extensive search of the area. The swimmer’s body has not been found. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Water police requested the shark be captured to assist with the recovery of potential coronial evidence. Police and fisheries officials remain in the area and nearby beaches are still closed. “My deepest condolences are with the family and loved ones of the 63-year-old man who tragically lost his life at Sorrento Beach yesterday,” Jarvis said. “This is an incredibly sad and distressing incident and my thoughts are with everyone involved.” Locals were urged to stay out of the water until the beach was declared safe for swimming. The local state MP, Liam Staltari, extended his condolences to the man’s family, friends and loved ones. “Like all locals and people from across WA, I’m deeply saddened by the tragic death of a man following today’s shark attack at Sorrento beach,” he said. “Our entire community is thinking of you at this incredibly difficult time.” A witness, Darrel Haythornthwaite, told 7News that he could not believe the incident had occurred, “especially in a place like this”. He said the man’s friend, who was swimming with him, made it back to shore but was inconsolable. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “He felt bad because he didn’t go back to save his mate and I said, ‘Nah you couldn’t have done that’,” he told the outlet. “There’s nothing that anyone could have done.” Another witness, Ingrid Mitchell, told 9News she swam at the beach every day and did not expect sharks to attack outside dawn and dusk. “There was other swimmers in there … just near the seaweed, and there was one poor girl there who was sunbaking, and she saw the whole lot as well,” she said. A third witness, Jacqui Rapaic, told the ABC she was walking along the beach with a friend when the incident occurred. “My friend said, ‘Jac, I think there’s been a shark attack,’ and I looked out to the ocean and I could see a pool of blood,” she said. “I hugged on to my friend … [we] felt rather traumatised at that point. It happened so quickly.” The fatality followed a shark attack on Monday at the remote Glenfield beach, north of Geraldton on WA’s mid-west coast, which left a surfer with serious injuries. He was taken to the nearby Geraldton health campus and was in a stable condition. – with AAP Explore more on these topics Western Australia Sharks Marine life Perth news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.aktuality.sk/clanok/AFnZ6Nr/.text: Švédsky parlament v stredu schválil ústavnú zmenu, ktorá umožní odobrať dvojaké občianstvo osobám, ktoré ho získali podvodom alebo boli odsúdené za trestné činy ohrozujúce švédske štátne záujmy, informovala agentúra AFP, píše TASR.Za túto zmenu hlasovalo 292 poslancov, proti ich bolo 51. Keďže voľby nepriniesli jednoznačný výsledok a politické strany stále rokujú o zostavení vlády, konkrétny návrh zákona na jej vykonanie bude musieť predložiť až nový kabinet.HeadingBlockOdoberanie občianstvaPodľa schválenej zmeny bude možné odobrať švédske občianstvo osobám s dvojakým občianstvom, ak ho získali na základe nepravdivých údajov alebo boli odsúdené za trestné činy, ktoré vážne poškodzujú životné záujmy Švédska.Odchádzajúca stredopravá vláda premiéra Ulfa Kristerssona vlani oznámila, že zvažuje odoberanie občianstva osobám s dvojakým občianstvom odsúdeným v prípadoch organizovaného zločinu a činnosti gangov. Na zavedenie takéhoto opatrenia bola potrebná zmena ústavy, ktorú musí parlament schváliť dvakrát, pričom medzi hlasovaniami sa musia konať voľby.
